challenges.name: entities-relationships-quiz
challenges.title: Lists in a column and facts about a pair
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the CodeDev student_ids incident: the query behind the My courses page, and a user story that needs an enrollment date. Decide whether each statement is True or False.

questions.question:
Schema v1 stores the learners of each course in one text column:

id | title                        | student_ids
---+------------------------------+------------
12 | SQL & Data Modeling          | 3,17,27,70
13 | Web Application Fundamentals | 7,8

The My courses page runs:

SELECT id, title FROM courses WHERE student_ids LIKE '%7%';

Statement: "For learner 7, this query returns exactly the courses learner 7 is enrolled in."
questions.explanation: False. LIKE '%7%' matches the character 7 anywhere in the text, so course 12 matches because of 17, 27 and 70, although learner 7 is only in course 13. Patching the pattern (for example with commas around the id) only moves the problem: the root cause is a list stored in one value, which the database cannot index, check against users or update one element at a time. The fix is a join table, enrollments(user_id, course_id, ...), queried with WHERE user_id = 7.

questions.question:
User stories:
- A learner can enroll in many courses.
- A course can have many learners.
- Admins need to see when each learner enrolled in each course.

Proposed schema:

users(id, email)
courses(id, title)
enrollments(user_id, course_id, enrolled_at, status)  -- primary key (user_id, course_id)

Statement: "enrolled_at belongs in enrollments rather than in users or courses, because it describes one learner in one course."
questions.explanation: True. A learner enrolls in many courses and a course has many learners, so one date column on users or on courses cannot hold one date per pair. The enrollment date is a fact about the relationship, and a many-to-many relationship with its own facts gets its own table: enrollments, with one row per learner and course. A common mistake is users.enrolled_at, which silently keeps only one date (usually the latest) for a learner with several courses.
